title: Concentrations in a two compartment model

segs.text: Module two, objective six. Predicting drug concentration after an I V bolus in a multi compartment model. For a two compartment drug, the plasma concentration is the sum of two falling exponential terms. C p equals A e to the minus alpha t, plus B e to the minus beta t. The alpha term is the fast one, for distribution, and the beta term is the slow one, for elimination. Alpha is always the larger exponent, because distribution is faster than elimination, but the intercepts A and B can be either way round. At time zero both exponentials equal one, so C p zero equals A plus B. She gives you the four parameters, and you substitute them.

card.m: a: distribution, fast; b: elimination, slow
a > b always; A and B either way

segs.text: Her deck practice uses theophylline: C p equals twelve e to the minus five point eight t, plus eighteen e to the minus zero point one six t. What is the plasma level three hours after an I V bolus dose? Read the parameters: A is twelve milligrams per liter, alpha is five point eight per hour, B is eighteen milligrams per liter, and beta is zero point one six per hour. Alpha is much larger than beta, as it must be. At time zero, twelve plus eighteen gives thirty milligrams per liter.

card.m: A = 12 mg/L, a = 5.8 hr<sup>−1</sup>; B = 18 mg/L, b = 0.16 hr<sup>−1</sup>

segs.text: Now each term at three hours. The distribution term is twelve times e to the minus five point eight times three, which is twelve times e to the minus seventeen point four. That is effectively zero milligrams per liter. The elimination term is eighteen times e to the minus zero point one six times three, which is eighteen times e to the minus zero point four eight. That exponential is zero point six one eight eight, so the term is eleven point one four milligrams per liter. Adding the two terms, zero plus eleven point one four gives eleven point one four milligrams per liter.

The elimination half-life of a two compartment drug is the beta half-life, and it comes from beta alone. The beta half-life equals zero point six nine three divided by beta. Do not calculate k first; divide zero point six nine three by beta directly. For theophylline, zero point six nine three over zero point one six per hour gives four point three three hours. Per hour in the bottom leaves hours. Using alpha here is the usual mistake.

The same four numbers give the rate constants of the model, all in per hour. Each uses the cross term, A times beta plus B times alpha, in which each intercept is multiplied by the other phase's slope, so work it out once. The overall elimination constant k equals alpha times beta times A plus B, divided by the cross term. It is a different number from beta. k two one equals the cross term divided by A plus B. k one two equals A times B times the square of beta minus alpha, divided by A plus B times the cross term. All three are on the equation sheet.

The volumes come next. The central volume, V p, equals the dose D zero divided by A plus B. Milligrams over milligrams per liter leaves liters. When a dose and an area under the curve are given instead, V p equals D zero divided by k times A U C from zero to infinity. The tissue volume, V t, equals V p times k one two, divided by k two one.

Her in-class sheet: a two hundred fifty milligram bolus, A eight point four five and B five point three two milligrams per liter, alpha two point one eight and beta zero point one one four per hour. The beta half-life is zero point six nine three over beta, six point zero eight hours. C p zero is A plus B, thirteen point seven seven milligrams per liter. The four hour alpha term is eight point four five times e to the minus two point one eight times four, zero point zero zero one. The beta term is five point three two times e to the minus zero point one one four times four, three point three seven two milligrams per liter. Adding gives three point three seven milligrams per liter.

The central volume is two hundred fifty milligrams over thirteen point seven seven milligrams per liter, which is eighteen point one six liters. The cross term is eight point four five times zero point one one four, which is zero point nine six three three, plus five point three two times two point one eight, which is eleven point five nine seven six. Together that is twelve point five six zero nine. Then k is two point one eight times zero point one one four times thirteen point seven seven, which is three point four two two one, divided by twelve point five six zero nine. That gives k of zero point two seven two per hour.

k two one is twelve point five six zero nine over thirteen point seven seven, which is zero point nine one two per hour. For k one two, the top is eight point four five times five point three two times the square of zero point one one four minus two point one eight, which is one hundred ninety one point eight eight. The bottom is thirteen point seven seven times twelve point five six zero nine, which is one hundred seventy two point nine six. So k one two is one point one zero nine per hour. Her questions give only the equation or the four parameters, and ask, in order, the elimination half-life, the initial concentration, a concentration at a stated hour and the central volume.
